summary: Lets IKEv2 peers get certificate revocation status using OCSP instead of in-band certificate revocation lists, which can grow without bound. OCSP responses are small and have a bounded size.

eli5.summary: To check that a certificate is still good, the old way sent a huge list of bad ones. This lets the other side send a short note saying yes this one is still fine.

questions: why not use crl in ikev2
how does ikev2 check certificate revocation
subtitle: How IKEv2 peers can swap a small OCSP answer instead of a huge revocation list to prove a certificate is still good.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 can carry certificate revocation lists in-band, but a list can grow without bound and a multi-megabyte file is impractical in an IKE exchange, so revocation checks tend to get skipped.
tldr.mechanism: A new CERT Encoding value, OCSP Content (14), lets a CERTREQ payload ask for an OCSP response and name trusted OCSP responders. The recipient answers with a CERT payload that holds the DER-encoded OCSP response.
tldr.outcome: Peers can check revocation status inside the IKEv2 handshake with a small, bounded-size message, even when a firewall stops them from reaching the OCSP responder directly.

today: RFC 4806 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the IKEv2 protocol of RFC 4306.

sections.title: The Revocation Problem in IKEv2
sections.content:
IKEv2 supports public key authentication, and confirming that a certificate is still reliable depends on knowing its revocation status. The traditional way is a Certificate Revocation List (CRL), and IKEv2 allows CRLs to be sent in-band in the CERT payload.

But CRLs can grow unbounded. The RFC notes that many real examples show the impracticality of putting a multi-megabyte file in an IKE exchange, especially in bandwidth-limited places such as mobile communications. The result is that CRLs are left out and fetched out-of-band, if they are used at all. Out-of-band access can even deadlock when reaching the CRL needs IPsec, and so IKE, to be working already. That pushes people toward blind trust in place of real revocation checks.

The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP, RFC 2560) is an alternative whose responses are bounded and small. This document defines an extension that carries them in-band. It applies when OCSP is wanted but security policy stops one IKEv2 peer from reaching the OCSP responder directly, as when firewalls keep outside peers away from an enterprise network.
sections.eli5: A giant list of cancelled cards is too heavy to carry, and sometimes you cannot even get to the list. A short note is easy to hand over.

sections.title: The OCSP Content Encoding
sections.content:
The extension adds one value to the Cert Encoding field of the IKEv2 CERT payload: OCSP Content, value 14. It is used in two ways.

In a CERTREQ payload (the "OCSP request"), it signals that the sender supports the extension and wants an OCSP confirmation in a later CERT payload. It also carries zero or more OCSP responder certificate hashes in the Certificate Authority field, which identify the OCSP responders the sender trusts. RFC 2560 lists three kinds of responder: the CA that issued the certificate, a Trusted Responder whose key the requester trusts, and a CA Designated Responder. Hashes matter only for the Trusted Responder case. For the CA itself they are not needed, and for a Designated Responder the requester does not know the key in advance.

In a CERT payload (the "OCSP response"), the same value means the Certificate Data field holds an OCSP response. It can be matched to the certificate it covers by the response's CertID field.
sections.eli5: The number 14 is a label that says "this is about a status note". One side asks for it, and the other side sends it.

sections.title: Rules for Requesters and Responders
sections.content:
An OCSP request is sent in its own CERTREQ payload, separate from other CERTREQs, because IKEv2 gives no way to tell which of several concatenated hashes belongs to an OCSP responder. If several responders are named, their hashes are concatenated and computed the same way as trust anchor hashes in RFC 4306, Section 3.7. When the requester gets the matching OCSP response, it SHALL feed it into the path validation logic of RFC 3280.

The recipient of an OCSP request SHOULD obtain the related OCSP assertion and send an OCSP response in a CERT payload, again separate from any other CERT payload. The response covers the certificate needed to verify its signature on IKEv2 payloads. How it gets the response is out of scope. The Certificate Data field SHALL hold a DER-encoded OCSPResponse structure from RFC 2560.

No reply to an OCSP request may just mean the peer does not support the extension. Nodes should be configured to require a response only if all peers are known to support it. Otherwise they should try OCSP and fall back to some other way of checking revocation.
sections.eli5: If you ask for a status note and get nothing back, maybe the other side does not know how. So you only insist on one when you know they can give it.

sections.title: Message Exchanges
sections.content:
In the peer-to-peer exchange, the Responder's second message carries an OCSP request CERTREQ. The Initiator replies in message 3 with its certificate, a separate CERT payload holding an OCSP response for that certificate, and its own OCSP request CERTREQ. Message 4 returns the Responder's certificate and a separate OCSP response for it.

The RFC points out that the Responder in message 2 does not yet have the Initiator's certificate, so it cannot build a normal OCSP request. Hashes are used instead, and the OCSP request is just an index into that data. So an OCSP response can be produced without a matching request, as long as OCSP nonces are not used.

The second scenario uses EAP for many end users reaching an enterprise IPsec gateway. OCSP checks only the server-side IKEv2 certificate, not certificates used inside EAP methods. The Initiator sends the OCSP request CERTREQ in message 3, and the Responder returns its certificate and OCSP response in message 4. Messages 5 through 8 are not relevant to this document, and where the examples conflict with RFC 4306, that RFC dominates.
sections.eli5: Both sides swap their ID card and a fresh status note at the same time, so each can check the other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the OCSP request here is not a real OCSP request, it cannot carry the nonce extension that RFC 2560 offers against replay attacks. RFC 2560 handles this by allowing pre-produced responses, but it warns that precomputed responses allow a replay of an old good response after the certificate has been revoked but before the response expires.

Deployments should weigh that benefit against the chance and cost of a replay. Nodes SHOULD make the required freshness of an OCSP response configurable.
sections.eli5: A status note made yesterday might be out of date today. So you should be able to choose how fresh a note has to be.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document defines one new value for the IKEv2 Cert Encoding field of the Certificate Payload. IANA has assigned OCSP Content the value 14 in the Cert Encoding table of RFC 4306, Section 3.6.
sections.eli5: The official list of labels now has a new entry: number 14 means a status note.
